spot.title: Imagination Park
spot.subtitle: Yoda, Indiana Jones, and George Lucas's gift

locating.anchor: the small fountain plaza beside San Anselmo Town Hall, a block off the boulevard toward downtown

document.text: There is a bit of movie magic hiding one block away, in the heart of downtown San Anselmo. Next to Town Hall sits a pocket park called Imagination Park, and keeping watch over its fountain are two bronze figures: Yoda, all two and a half feet of Jedi master, and Indiana Jones, standing six-foot-three with whip in hand. George Lucas, a longtime San Anselmo resident, made it happen. In twenty thirteen he donated a parcel of land he owned downtown, paid to clear away the old commercial buildings on it, and gave the town both statues. They were sculpted by Lawrence Noble, an artist who worked with the Lucasfilm team on the second Star Wars film. Lucas said he wanted a place where children and adults could pause for a moment of peace and, with luck, a little inspiration. Judging by the kids climbing on Yoda most afternoons, it worked.

spot.title: Marin Art and Garden Center
spot.subtitle: Eleven acres the women of Marin saved

locating.anchor: the leafy hedge and gateway of the garden center at Laurel Grove Avenue

document.text: Behind the hedge along the boulevard in Ross lie eleven acres with a remarkable story. This land was once part of Rancho Punta de Quentin, a Mexican land grant bought in eighteen fifty-nine by James Ross, the Scottish merchant the town is named for. His daughter Annie and her husband George Worn made their homestead here, and in eighteen sixty-four built an eight-sided, two-story wellhouse that is still standing. When development threatened the estate after World War Two, a determined group of Marin women led by conservationist Caroline Livermore bought it, and in nineteen forty-five created the Marin Art and Garden Center. The mansion itself is gone, but a fairy ring of magnolias still grows where its great magnolia once stood, alongside a dawn redwood and a giant sequoia. In twenty twenty-two the entire garden was added to the National Register of Historic Places.

spot.title: Corte Madera Creek
spot.subtitle: A concrete channel with wild steelhead in it

locating.anchor: the wide green waterway running alongside the boulevard

document.text: The waterway threading beside the boulevard is Corte Madera Creek, and it leads a double life. After decades of floods in the Ross Valley, the Army Corps of Engineers straightened the creek's lower miles in the late nineteen-sixties and lined this stretch with concrete. Yet it remains a living stream. Every winter, wild steelhead trout swim in from San Francisco Bay and fight their way up this very channel to spawn in the gravel hills upstream. For years the smooth concrete was almost too much for them; the water ran so fast that exhausted fish were simply swept back downstream. Engineers and local creek volunteers have been reworking the channel with resting pools and better fish passage so more of the spawners make it home. Keep an eye on the water: the tide pushes all the way up here, and egrets and herons patrol the shallows.

spot.title: The Roller Coaster Bridge
spot.subtitle: Five and a half miles of humps and dips since 1956

locating.anchor: the double-humped bridge deck stretching across the water ahead

document.text: Get ready for one of the strangest bridges in America. The Richmond–San Rafael Bridge stretches about five and a half miles across the bay, and it rises and dips like a roller coaster. That's no accident: it has to clear two separate shipping channels, so engineers built two identical steel humps — one hundred eighty-five feet and one hundred thirty-five feet of clearance — and let the deck sag in between to save steel. When it opened on September first, nineteen fifty-six, it replaced a ferry line that had carried cars across since nineteen fifteen. Critics were rough on its looks; the architect Frank Lloyd Wright famously despised it. Locals grew fond of it anyway. And after more than six decades as a cars-only crossing, a protected path opened on the upper deck in twenty nineteen, letting cyclists and walkers travel between Marin and Contra Costa counties for the very first time.

spot.title: The Brothers
spot.subtitle: A working lighthouse you can sleep in

locating.anchor: the two small rocky islets with the white Victorian lighthouse

document.text: Out in the open water sit two small rocky islets called The Brothers — and on the larger one, a Victorian lighthouse has kept watch since eighteen seventy-four. East Brother Light Station marks the narrow, foggy strait where San Francisco Bay squeezes into San Pablo Bay, a bottleneck that once claimed ships with grim regularity. When the Coast Guard automated the light in nineteen sixty-nine, the government planned to tear the old keeper's house down. Neighbors refused to let that happen. They formed a nonprofit, restored the gingerbread woodwork by hand, and in nineteen eighty reopened the island as one of the most unusual bed-and-breakfasts anywhere: guests ride a small boat out, climb the tower at sunset, and spend the night surrounded by water on every side. The light itself still shines after a hundred and fifty years — tended now by innkeepers instead of keepers.

spot.title: Castro Rocks
spot.subtitle: Harbor seals beneath the bridge

locating.anchor: the string of low rocks at the base of the bridge piers

document.text: Just beside the bridge piers, a string of low rocks barely clears the water — and at low tide they are crowded with harbor seals. This is Castro Rocks, the largest harbor seal rookery in the northern part of San Francisco Bay, where dozens of seals haul out to rest, warm up, and, each spring, give birth to their pups. The rocks are named for Don Víctor Castro, a Californio ranchero whose family once held this shoreline, and they have appeared on nautical charts since a survey in eighteen fifty. The seals are such established residents that when engineers seismically retrofitted the bridge, federal wildlife authorities issued special permits and rules so the construction would not drive them away. So somewhere below the roadway at this very moment, there is a good chance a seal is dozing in the sun, utterly unbothered by the traffic overhead.

spot.title: The Albany Bulb
spot.subtitle: A landfill that turned into an art park

locating.anchor: the scrubby green peninsula poking out into the bay

document.text: That knob of land reaching into the bay is not natural at all. It is a pile of broken buildings. From nineteen sixty-three to nineteen eighty-three, this was Albany's dump for construction debris, concrete, rebar, rubble, and asphalt, heaped into the water until a lawsuit shut it down. Then something wonderful happened: nature and artists moved in together. Wildflowers and coyote brush swallowed the rubble, and starting in the nineteen nineties, self-taught sculptors began building strange and beautiful things from whatever washed up or stuck out of the ground. The most famous is the Beseeching Woman, a fifteen-foot figure with her arms flung wide toward the Golden Gate, made by a civil rights attorney named Osha Neumann. The Bulb has hosted driftwood castles, painted concrete slabs, and years of debate about what a wild, unplanned place should become. It remains one of the East Bay's oddest and best-loved shorelines.

spot.title: Serpentine
spot.subtitle: Riding on the ocean floor

locating.anchor: the rocky switchbacks of the Serpentine Trail

document.text: The Serpentine Trail is named twice over: for its switchbacks, and for the smooth green-gray rock they cut through. Serpentine is California's state rock, and the story of how it got here is enormous. This ridge is part of the Franciscan complex, the crumpled leftovers of an ocean floor that spent millions of years diving beneath North America. Some slabs of the deep crust and upper mantle were scraped off instead of swallowed, soaked in seawater, and transformed into serpentinite, which now caps ridges all through these hills. The rock makes harsh soil, low in nutrients and laced with heavy metals, so ordinary plants struggle. What grows instead is the lean chaparral around you, manzanita and chamise, with rare serpentine-adapted plants at the higher elevations and wildflowers blooming straight out of the weathered outcrops in spring. When the trail surface turns polished and slick under your tires, that is the mantle of the earth you are sliding on.

The name honors James and Thomas Roy, brothers from Vermont who acquired four hundred twenty acres in eighteen seventy-seven when a twenty-thousand-dollar loan went unpaid, and who ran a dairy ranch here. Marin County's Open Space District bought the land in nineteen seventy-eight. For decades this ranch bred and trained Morgans and supplied them to national parks across the country. At its height the herd numbered thirty-five to forty horses, and rangers came here to learn horsemanship. The breeding program wound down in the late nineteen nineties as parks began keeping their own stables, but the horses never left. A small herd still works this seashore today, carrying rangers on backcountry patrol, helping with search and rescue, counting harbor seals along the shore, tallying tule elk, and packing trash off the trails. Stop by the corrals and you may meet a four-legged park ranger on its day off.

spot.subtitle: Middle schoolers and willow walls

locating.anchor: the creek corridor running alongside Olema Road

document.text: Fairfax Creek runs through this neighborhood on its way down from the ridges above town, and this stretch is where the community started giving it back its health. In the fall of two thousand four, the Friends of Corte Madera Creek teamed up with science classes at White Hill Middle School just upstream, pulling out invasive broom and non-native blackberry along the banks and replacing them with native plants. Three years later a conservation corps crew planted seven hundred more natives and wove a living willow wall and a willow mattress into the bank — erosion control that sprouts leaves. The creek showed its power soon after: very heavy rain in January of two thousand eight sent floodwater over Olema Road at number three hundred, and that summer the undersized culvert there was dug out and replaced with a bigger one. Restoration here is patient, hand-scale work — kids with shovels, willows doing engineering — betting that a small creek can be a living one again.

spot.title: Restless Ground
spot.subtitle: Why every Fairfax hillside got a report card

locating.anchor: the steep wooded hillside streets climbing above the flats

document.text: The hills wrapped around Fairfax are made of the Franciscan Complex — old ocean floor scraped off a sinking tectonic plate over a hundred million years ago and shoved onto the edge of the continent. It is a jumble of graywacke sandstone, shale, ribbon chert, basalt, and slippery serpentinite, all sheared together into what geologists call a melange. That chaotic rock is why the town sits in a bowl of steep slopes, and it is also why the slopes move. Fairfax's landslide troubles got so notorious that in late nineteen seventy-two the state's Division of Mines and Geology sent a geologist to spend a year inventorying every single parcel in town, rating each site from one to four for slide susceptibility. Those horrendous slide problems are a big reason the town later protected its hillsides and ridgelines from development. When you see a tilted fence or a rippled road up here, you are watching geology happen — the seafloor under Fairfax, still settling in.

And every drop that lands on those slopes has exactly one exit: San Anselmo Creek, the stream threading this valley beside the road, which supplies an estimated ninety percent of the water in Corte Madera Creek downstream. The creek lives a double life. In the drought of nineteen seventy-seven it dried up completely, a bed of bare cobbles. Between nineteen fourteen and nineteen sixty, the valley averaged a damaging flood roughly every four years. Nearly everything you will hear along this stretch of road, the buried creeks, the ballot-box battles, the bridges bought just to be torn down, flows from one stubborn fact: the Ross Valley is a funnel, and the towns were built at the bottom of it.

spot.title: The Fish Behind the School
spot.subtitle: Ocean-going trout still spawn in the creek that wraps Archie Williams High

locating.anchor: the Archie Williams High School campus fronting Sir Francis Drake Boulevard, with San Anselmo Creek curving behind the school buildings

document.text: San Anselmo Creek makes a lazy curve behind Archie Williams High School, and near Saunders Avenue it swallows a tributary running down out of Sleepy Hollow. In August it is a shaded trickle you could step across. But in winter, this is a steelhead stream. Steelhead are rainbow trout with wanderlust. Born in gravel like this, they ride high water down to San Francisco Bay and out to the ocean, grow big and silver on a saltwater diet, then fight their way home, under the Golden Gate, up Corte Madera Creek, and into this channel behind a public high school. Between January and April a female picks the top of a riffle, turns on her side, and beats a nest into the gravel, called a redd, where she lays her eggs. The finest spawning gravels in the whole watershed lie in the upper reaches of San Anselmo, Sleepy Hollow, and Ross creeks. These fish are survivors of a vanishing tribe, one of only a handful of small steelhead populations still hanging on in San Francisco Bay tributaries. Every culvert and concrete drop between here and the bay is a hurdle; in two thousand five, biologists walked these creeks cataloguing every single barrier, crossing by crossing, trying to keep the way home open.

spot.title: Muir Beach Overlook Coastal Defenses
spot.subtitle: National park history and nature

document.text: Beyond our Muir Beach destination, the nearby overlook preserves four little concrete rooms that soldiers nicknamed gopher holes. During World War Two, these observation posts helped defend San Francisco Bay. Two men kept watch in each station, tracking ships through powerful telescopes and relaying bearings to plotting crews. By comparing observations from separate posts, those crews could locate targets offshore and calculate instructions for coastal guns. The work required patience in cramped quarters: typically one room, two narrow bunks, and a stove. The Army also rented village cabins for housing and a cookhouse.

document.text: At Muir Beach, a crab census can become a science lesson. The beach beyond our parking-lot destination has been a monitoring site for LiMPETS since 2002. Those counts focus attention on an animal with an important place in the sandy beach food web. Mole crabs are major plant eaters along the Pacific coasts of both North and South America, giving student observers a small subject with a much larger ecological role.
